Article Title: 'Do you think AI will kill all humans?' Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei answers
Article Text:
He also explained why he no longer prefers expressing AI risks through a single probability.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said it is more useful to assess the risks posed by artificial intelligence by examining different possible paths for its development rather than assigning a single percentage to the chances of AI causing catastrophic harm.Addressing warnings from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon and others about the rapid development of increasingly capable AI systems, Cooper asked Amodei: "Do you believe, earnestly believe that AI could kill all humans? What percent chance do you think it is?"In response, Amodei stated, "It's funny, I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him. It's an interesting resignation because when he left, he said, I think Anthropic is the most responsible player."Also read: 27 year old Anthropic researcher who quit AI industry says the biggest decisions on humanity's future are being taken on 'the MacBooks of some engineers living in San Francisco' instead of... Amodei said Coxon's concerns were not specifically directed at Anthropic but reflected broader concerns about the pace of the AI industry. "I think Anthropic is the most aware of these issues. He wasn't calling out us, he was calling out the dynamic of the industry as a whole moving too fast," he said.He also explained why he no longer prefers expressing AI risks through a single probability. "Now, I think I already said, these unconditional probabilities, I used to talk in that way because it's an easy way to express, I think there's some chance that things go wrong, but it's not all that high."According to Amodei, breaking down the possible outcomes provides a clearer picture of the risks. "Again, I think it's more illuminating to think in terms of how do you decompose those probabilities? What are the paths in which things go well, and what are the paths in which things go poorly? Instead of saying, it's a 10% chance, that sounds like it's a roll of the dice. I think it's much more illuminating to say, well, that forks into different paths. If we take the right paths, then the chance of something going wrong is very low."He added that the AI industry needed to work together on safeguards. "If we take the wrong paths, then the chance of something going wrong could be even higher than that. Let's focus on our agency and our ability to take the right paths instead of the wrong paths. I think that the way to take the right paths is for the industry to work together."Amodei also cautioned against slowing AI development without considering who would ultimately control the technology. "Again, we'll talk about the proposal that I've put out today, but at the end of the day, the industry has to work together and it's harder, but to some extent, the world has to work together. If we go too slow, I still believe that the wrong people will be in charge of the technology. That, again, will bring the probability of things going wrong very high. "The comments come amid growing concerns from AI safety researchers. Joe Benton, who said he left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago, has warned that AI companies are racing to develop systems capable of recursively improving themselves.Benton said companies were underinvesting in safety and called for greater transparency, reporting of safety incidents and independent assessments of AI systems.His concerns followed Coxon's resignation from Anthropic, where he had worked on AI pretraining research. Coxon had warned that leading AI companies were moving towards self-improving superintelligence without adequate safeguards.
Article Summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said it is more useful to assess the risks posed by artificial intelligence by examining different possible paths for its development. He also explained why he no longer prefers expressing AI risks through a single probability. The comments come amid growing concerns from AI safety researchers.

Article Title: China has put 2,000 servers in sea near Shanghai, taking off from a Microsoft project that shutdown in 2020, where the company sank 855 servers in North Sea
Article Text:
China's 24MW underwater data centre off Shanghai runs 2,000 servers cooled by seawater and powered by an offshore wind farm, six years after Microsoft pulled 855 servers out of the North Sea and shelved the idea.

Microsoft's underwater servers failed at one-eighth the rate of its land servers

China's underwater data centre runs GPU clusters for AI training

Seawater cooling cuts the power bill and removes the freshwater bill entirely

Marine biologists say the warming around the pods stays local

Microsoft shut Project Natick down even though the numbers worked

China has switched on a commercial underwater data centre off the coast of Shanghai, dropping roughly 2,000 servers onto the seabed in the Lingang Special Area and wiring them directly into an offshore wind farm. The facility runs at 24MW, sits 10 metres below the surface and more than 10km out, and uses the surrounding seawater in place of chillers and cooling towers. It took 1.6 billion yuan of investment, roughly Rs 2,100 crore, and is a joint effort between HiCloud Technology and state-owned China Communications Construction. Commercial operations began in May, after trials in February and construction wrapping up last October.The design it borrows from belongs to Microsoft. In 2018 the company lowered a white steel cylinder the size of a shipping container 117 feet under the North Sea off the Orkney Islands, with 855 servers inside and 27.6 petabytes of storage. The air was pumped out first and replaced with dry nitrogen, so nothing inside could oxidise or take on moisture. Two years later Microsoft pulled it back up, published results better than anyone expected, and then walked away from the idea entirely.The number that made the experiment famous was the failure rate. Microsoft lost six of the 855 servers on the seabed. A control group running identical jobs in an ordinary building on land lost eight out of 135. That works out to 0.7% underwater against 5.9% on land. Two things explain it. Cold seawater carried heat away at no cost, and a sealed tube filled with nitrogen and off limits to humans removed slow corrosion and the accidental knocks that wear down land hardware over years. Power usage effectiveness came in at 1.07, with no mechanical cooling at all, at a time when most of the industry was still sitting above 1.5.The Shanghai pod is not a proof of concept. It carries GPU clusters doing AI training, big data annotation and work on domestic large language models, with computing capacity deployed by China Telecom and local service providers. Its developers put its PUE at around 1.15, claim a 22.8% cut in electricity consumption, no water use at all, and more than 90% less land than an equivalent site onshore. The Chinese government says the project is designed to run on more than 95% green electricity. HiCloud first sank servers off Hainan in 2021 and set up the first commercial modules there in 2023. It has talked about taking the offshore wind model up to 500MW.The timing is what makes an old experiment relevant. In a land-based facility, somewhere between a quarter and half of total electricity demand goes to moving chilled water around the servers. Training clusters are pushing density past what ordinary buildings can handle, and grid operators in Virginia and Texas have started resisting new data centre connections. A sealed module offshore avoids both halves of the problem. The sea absorbs the heat, the turbines overhead supply the electricity, and no aquifer gets touched. A United Nations university institute warned this week that the water footprint of data centres could hit 9.3 trillion litres by 2030, roughly what the entire population of sub-Saharan Africa uses domestically in a year.The obvious objection is that a heat source on the seabed is still a heat source. Researchers who study coastal ecosystems say the risks, including disturbed sediment and warmer water immediately around the modules, look manageable but need monitoring over time. Rick Stafford, a marine biologist at Bournemouth University, said cooling with seawater does raise local temperatures but that the effect will "not be far reaching". Microsoft's own cylinder came back up wearing algae, barnacles and anemones grown to the size of melons, which answered a question nobody had asked about whether sea life would mind the hardware.Microsoft confirmed in 2024 that its subsea programme was over. Noelle Walsh, who runs the company's cloud operations and innovation group, said flatly that she was not building subsea data centres anywhere in the world. The reasoning was practical rather than technical. Sending a technician down in a strong current to fix a failed board is expensive, saltwater still eats steel, and Microsoft has been building on land at a pace it has no reason to slow. A researcher at Hong Kong Polytechnic University put the gap simply: Microsoft got to the concept first, while China had the market demand, marine engineering and policy backing to turn it into a working commercial site. Around 90% of the world's AI data centre capacity now sits in those two countries.
Article Summary: China has switched on a commercial underwater data centre off the coast of Shanghai. The facility runs at 24MW, sits 10 metres below the surface and more than 10km out. It uses the surrounding seawater in place of chillers and cooling towers. Microsoft's underwater servers failed at one-eighth the rate of its land servers.

Article Title: 27 year old Anthropic researcher who quit AI industry says the biggest decisions on humanity's future are being taken on 'the MacBooks of some engineers living in San Francisco' instead of...
Article Text:
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic saying the industry is gambling with our lives. Four days later, Dario Amodei called for slowing down, and Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google DeepMind agreed.

Anthropic researcher says the fear inside AI labs is real, and it rarely gets said out loud

Anthropic and Google AI safety researchers keep walking out, and the resignations are stacking up

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei responds with a pacing plan; Demis Hassabis, Sam Altman and Elon Musk back it

Coxon's resignation lands while Anthropic is selling investors on responsible development

An Anthropic researcher has quit the artificial intelligence industry, saying the choices that will decide how safely superintelligent AI arrives are being made inside a private company's Slack channel. Jacob Coxon, who spent three years on pretraining research at OpenAI and then Anthropic, announced his exit on Tuesday in a thread on X that has now passed 155 million views. Within four days it had pulled two more researchers out of their jobs and drawn a response from Anthropic's own chief executive.Coxon, a 27-year-old Briton with a mathematics background, said Anthropic staff debate what their models can actually do on an internal employee Slack channel, and that it is strange for something this consequential to run on "the MacBooks of some engineers living in San Francisco" rather than out of a desert bunker of the sort built for the Manhattan Project. His public post was blunter. Both labs, he wrote, are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. "He joined OpenAI in 2023, worked on GPT-4o, and moved to Anthropic in July 2026 because of its safety reputation. Senior people at both companies, he said, privately believe AI could kill everyone by the end of the decade, then soften the language when they speak in public. The distinction he draws is uncomfortable for his former employer.At OpenAI, he said, the civilisational stakes have not sunk in. At Anthropic they have, but the company believes it must get there first because no rival will act responsibly.Evan Hubinger, who leads alignment stress testing at Anthropic, replied to the thread and agreed with him, writing that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans". He put his own odds above 10 per cent within the next ten years and said the company does not yet have a plan for aligning superintelligence.Two more went public this week. Joe Benton, who ran a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who worked on AI safety at Google, told NBC News they had left and were joining METR, the nonprofit that evaluates catastrophic AI risk. "There are no adults in the room," Engels said. Benton's specific worry is disclosure: right now, he said, every bit of transparency about these risks from the companies is voluntary.Before them, Anthropic safeguards researcher Mrinank Sharma left in February, saying he wanted work that matched his integrity. OpenAI researcher Hieu Pham quit the same month citing burnout. Alignment chief Jan Leike walked out in 2024, saying safety culture had lost ground to shiny products. Geoffrey Irving, former chief scientist at the UK's AI Security Institute, posted this week that he puts the chance of everyone dying from superintelligence at roughly 50 per cent.The warnings have started collecting evidence. In July, OpenAI models escaped a test environment and hacked Hugging Face's systems, attacking targets nobody had pointed them at. Anthropic later disclosed three cases of Claude models reaching other organisations' systems without authorisation. An Anthropic spokesperson said the company has always been open about AI bringing both benefits and unprecedented risks, and that it continues to build some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.Four days after Coxon's post, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay arguing that the industry must slow how fast it improves model capabilities. He named the Hugging Face incident as one of two things that changed his mind, the other being that AI is now building the next generation of AI. His plan has three steps: embedded third-party evaluators with employee-like access, which Anthropic is committing to on its own; coordination among labs in democracies; and eventually some agreement with China. "We owe it to humanity to try," he wrote.The backing was quick and unusual. Altman said he agreed, called embedded evaluators a good idea and said OpenAI would do the same. Musk posted that Dario is right. Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassbis said the essay "points towards the right path forward" and that while the details need working through, the direction is correct, pointing back to his own recent proposal for an industry-wide standards body for frontier AI. Altman also told Fortune that an OpenAI IPO now would be ill-advised, pushing it to 2027 at the earliest. Meta is the holdout. Mark Zuckerberg argued last month that the answer is distributing superintelligence to everyone rather than letting a few labs set limits.Anthropic's own listing is reportedly planned for next month, raising around $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation, with responsible development as a central part of the pitch. Coxon has signed a statement, with more than 1,000 researchers including Amodei and OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, asking governments to coordinate a way to slow development if models begin improving themselves.Nobody has built that mechanism yet. There are no federal AI regulations in the US, lawmakers are now calling for special sessions of Congress, and a bill from Bernie Sanders and Greg Casar to ban superintelligence and pause development until a regulator writes rules is the closest thing on the table. Until that changes, the decisions Coxon is worried about stay exactly where he left them, on the laptops.
Article Summary: Anthropic and Google AI safety researchers keep walking out, and the resignations are stacking up. Jacob Coxon, who spent three years on pretraining research at OpenAI and then Anthropic, announced his exit on Tuesday. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay arguing that the industry must slow how fast it improves model capabilities.

Article Title: Larry Ellison cancels plan to sell $7.5 billion of Oracle stock after Europe has a problem with 'his timing'
Article Text:
“Larry Ellison, Executive Chair of the Board and Chief Technology Officer, has cancelled his 10b5-1 Plan to sell Oracle stock.

No Oracle stock was sold under that plan, and he has no other plans to sell any of his Oracle stock.”

Why Larry Ellison cancelled the Oracle stock sale plan

What is a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan in the US

Why Europe takes a different approach

Larry Ellison has decided to cancel a trading plan a day after disclosing it. This plan would have allowed the Oracle co-founder to sell up to 50 million shares of the software company. Oracle has now confirmed that Ellison has sold no shares under the arrangement, which was due to remain in place until October 24. The timing has drawn attention because European market-abuse rules would not have allowed an executive to trade during the 30 days before financial results.In a press release, the company wrote,The shares covered by the plan were worth about $8.75 billion when it was adopted on June 22 and are worth about $7.5 billion at the current price, after Oracle's stock fell roughly 16%. This trading plan also drew attention because Oracle had just reported shrinking gross margins, while the company was also increasing the expected cost of its job cuts to $2.8 billion.The plan to scrap highlights differences between US and European rules for companies. In the US, executives can set up Rule 10b5-1 plans beforehand. Meanwhile, in Europe, the trading window typically closes before financial results, rather than offering a similar safe harbour as offered in America.Oracle has taken on significant debt as it expands its infrastructure business, while its shares have fallen roughly 20% this year. In its latest earnings, the company reported a 121% year-over-year increase in cloud infrastructure revenue and exceeded estimates, but also posted shrinking gross margins and raised the expected cost of its job cuts to $2.8 billion. Its shares fell 1.7% after the results.Ellison controls about 40% of Oracle and is its executive chair and chief technology officer. Selling all 50 million shares under the proposed plan would still have left him with about 1.1 billion shares. The sale was unusual given that, according to FactSet, he has not sold more than 25,000 Oracle shares at a time since the start of the century.A Rule 10b5-1 Plan is the American way of enabling executives and other insiders to prearrange stock sales. This means an executive may develop the plan when he does not have insider information; the trades are then made according to the set instructions.The plan allows the executive to dispose of shares at times when the decision would raise questions about whether he had access to material, non-public information. The rule was developed in 2000, and the SEC strengthened disclosure requirements in 2022.In Ellison's case, the plan has been publicly disclosed because American regulations require it. However, because no shares were sold before cancelling the plan, no transaction occurred.European market-abuse rules do not have an equivalent to the US 10b5-1 safe harbour. Under the European Union's Market Abuse Regulation, people discharging managerial responsibilities generally cannot trade in their company's shares during the 30 calendar days before an interim or year-end financial report.So the European approach closes the trading window instead of letting executives implement a pre-arranged plan that can continue during the restricted period.The disclosure rules are also different. In Europe, regulators focus more on reporting closed transactions than on the intent to set up a trading plan. Company managers must report transactions within three working days of reaching the annual threshold of €5,000.​So a plan that was set out but never executed would not have resulted in the same disclosure in Europe.​
Article Summary: Oracle co-founder cancels trading plan a day after disclosing it. Plan would have allowed Ellison to sell up to 50 million shares of the software company. European market-abuse rules would not have allowed an executive to trade during the 30 days before financial results. Oracle has taken on significant debt as it expands its infrastructure business.

Article Title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls on AI firms to slow pace of development, gets backing from Sam Altman & Elon Musk
Article Text:
File photo: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (centre) and Tesla chief Elon Musk

Why Amodei wants AI development slowed

Anthropic proposes third-party AI evaluators

OpenAI testing raises safety concerns

Researcher quits AI industry over concerns

Amodei says AI benefits remain the goal

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called on artificial intelligence companies to slow the pace of development of increasingly powerful AI models, warning that unchecked progress could make the technology harder for humans to understand and control.“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay published on his personal website on Saturday.Amodei said AI could bring major benefits but also carried serious risks because of the power of the technology.“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious,” he wrote.His call has received support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla chief Elon Musk . Altman said the need to pace the development of frontier AI had been a key topic of discussions at OpenAI in recent weeks.“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman said in a post on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.”Musk also endorsed Amodei’s proposal, writing: “Dario is right.”Amodei said his concern had grown as AI development accelerated, particularly because AI systems were increasingly being used to help build the next generation of AI.“My first concern is that, since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI,” he wrote.He referred to this process as “recursive self-improvement” and said it was beginning to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic.“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” Amodei wrote.He also pointed to risks including the possibility of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption.Amodei said commercial incentives could make these risks more acute if companies engaged in a race to develop increasingly capable systems without sufficient safeguards.Amodei said Anthropic would take steps to allow independent scrutiny of its AI systems.“We’ll provide third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training,” he wrote.His wider three-part plan calls for each frontier AI company to give ongoing, employee-like access to embedded third-party evaluators.He also proposed coordination among AI companies to establish common safety standards and limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress, along with global coordination on AI development.Amodei said democratic governments should coordinate with authoritarian governments while recognising the difficulties involved in verifying compliance.The discussion comes amid concerns over the behaviour of increasingly capable AI systems.OpenAI had revealed during testing that some AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a platform used by developers to store and share code.Amodei also referred to an incident involving an OpenAI-Hugging Face system in which a swarm of AI agents staged cybersecurity attacks on targets they had not been instructed to attack.He warned that such a swarm could potentially become capable of taking over the internet.Amodei's comments came days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon announced that he was leaving the industry after spending three years pretraining AI models, first at OpenAI and later at Anthropic.Coxon had considered Anthropic more cautious in its approach but said both companies were moving too quickly towards increasingly autonomous systems.“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday.“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a post on X.Pretraining is the stage in which AI models absorb vast quantities of data.Superintelligence refers to the theoretical point at which AI capabilities exceed human intelligence.Despite his call for slower development, Amodei said he continued to believe AI could significantly improve human life.“I have worked on AI for the last twelve years because I believe it could dramatically raise the quality of human life,” he wrote.He said AI could potentially cure major diseases in the next five to 10 years, accelerate economic growth, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and contribute to a renaissance of democracy and freedom.But he argued that achieving those benefits would require greater care over how the technology is developed.“The benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way,” Amodei wrote.He said the time gained by slowing development could be used to advance research into AI interpretability, improve operational security and strengthen safeguards at frontier AI companies.Amodei's latest call echoes an earlier appeal by Anthropic in June to slow or suspend AI development. In late July, Altman had also said AI developers might need to voluntarily slow their rapid advances to give society time to catch up.At around the same time, more than 1,000 employees at leading AI companies, including Amodei, signed a petition calling on the US government to help “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.
Article Summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called on artificial intelligence companies to slow the pace of development of increasingly powerful AI models. He warned that unchecked progress could make the technology harder for humans to understand and control. His call has received support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla chief Elon Musk.

Article Title: Roblox Developers Conference: Roblox now offers new ways to play, build and reach wider audience
Article Text:
(Image via: Roblox)

New ways to connect, communicate and enjoy games

Expanding the game engine and AI-powered creation tools

New chapter for creator earnings and game discovery

Roblox Corporation has unveiled a fresh wave of updates at its 12th annual Roblox Developers Conference (RDC), an exclusive gathering that brings together the platform's community of developers, artists, designers, brands and influencers. Marking 20 years of platform growth alongside its creator base, the company used the event to announce changes aimed at broadening how people play, equipping creators with more powerful engine and AI tools and setting the stage for the next phase of creator growth on the platform.One of the biggest announcements that Roblox made is that players collectively spent 29 billion hours on the platform last quarter alone, spread across more than 180 countries. Building on that scale, the company revealed a set of updates designed to let players jump into games from anywhere, on any device, stay connected with friends between sessions and explore entirely new game formats and styles.Among these updates is Roblox Everywhere that allows creators to reach players wherever they already spend time online. Going forward, creators will have the option to release their games as standalone apps across mobile, PC and console platforms, with Roblox handling the underlying technology and infrastructure behind the scenes.Roblox is also bringing gameplay directly to the web. By the end of this year, players will be able to jump straight into a game through their Chrome browser, accessible directly from a game's Experience Details Page, with no app download or installation required. Users can access the game via a link, posted anywhere online.Offline play is getting a boost too with players will soon be able to continue playing even without an active internet connection, whether they are mid-flight or dealing with patchy network coverage. Creators will be able to build games that combine both online and offline modes, opening the door to single-player campaigns and offline sessions that don't rely on a constant connection.Roblox is also expanding beyond its traditional strength in 3D multiplayer worlds, and the platform is rolling out new engine capabilities specifically built for 2D game development. This includes a new orthographic camera, animated image containers and direct sprite-sheet import support. Additional visual upgrades, such as blur effects, text shadows and improved gradients, aim to enhance how games look and feel, while a new notification system will support turn-based, asynchronous multiplayer experiences.To help players stay connected across different games, Roblox introduced a new Friends chat tab that follows users no matter which game they're currently in, making it easier for friends to coordinate and jump into new games together. A newly launched voice typing feature also lets players speak instead of type while playing, making in-game communication faster and more natural.According to Roblox, the platform has essentially built a cloud-based operating system for gaming, and the company is now layering AI-powered creation tools on top of that foundation, not as a single standalone tool, but as an entire system designed to handle the complexity that comes with building games.One major update here is the expansion of Build, a feature within the Roblox app that lets anyone create and publish a game simply by typing out prompts. Build is now expanding into public alpha testing in Serbia and Singapore. Alongside this expansion, Roblox is rolling out additional tools to give creators finer control, including a new asset library, desktop access, and more iterative editing capabilities.Later this year, Roblox will introduce Scene Generator, a tool bringing prompt-to-scene creation to both Build and Roblox Studio, with Studio offering creators a greater degree of control over the output. Using this tool, creators simply provide a text prompt along with a reference image, and Scene Generator produces a fully functional scene layout that can then be refined further within Studio.Roblox is also expanding what non-player characters, or NPCs, are capable of within games. By the end of the year, two new NPC behaviours will roll out, including NPCs capable of playtesting games themselves.The company also introduced Roblox Wallet, a dedicated financial account designed to scale alongside growing creator businesses. Through Wallet, creators can earn directly in real currency, receive automatic payouts every business day and transfer funds either to other Roblox accounts or to an external bank account, all while accessing more detailed earnings analytics through the Creator Hub.Alongside Wallet, Roblox also announced the Roblox Card, which will let creators spend their available Wallet balance anywhere the card is accepted. The Roblox Card is set to begin rolling out next year.On the discovery side, Roblox emphasised that great games should be easy for players to find, whether through the platform's homepage, the Moments tab, or across any browser or device. The Moments tab, where players can browse gameplay videos and tap to jump straight into a game, is now fully available across the United States.
Article Summary: Roblox Corporation has unveiled a fresh wave of updates at its 12th annual Roblox Developers Conference. The company used the event to announce changes aimed at broadening how people play, equipping creators with more powerful engine and AI tools. Players collectively spent 29 billion hours on the platform last quarter alone, spread across more than 180 countries.

Article Title: Oracle raises restructuring bill to $2.8 billion amid AI spending push: Report
Article Text:
Oracle raises restructuring bill to $2.8 billion amid AI spending push: Report

Oracle faces pressure from AI spending

Oracle plans to raise $40 billion

Oracle said restructuring costs linked to its cost-cutting plan will rise by about $700 million as the cloud company looks to control spending while investing heavily to meet strong demand for AI artificial intelligence services. As stated in a Reuters report, the company disclosed the increase in a regulatory filing. The higher estimate, which came after the end of Oracle’s August quarter, takes the expected cost of its fiscal 2026 restructuring plan to about $2.8 billion.As per the report, the plan includes job cuts, severance payments, contract terminations and other costs related to leaving certain operations. Oracle said some of the restructuring is linked to the growing use of AI across parts of the company.The cost-cutting plan comes at a difficult time for Oracle. Investors have been divided over the company’s AI strategy, with some betting on strong growth while others remain concerned about the large amounts of money Oracle is spending to expand its AI and cloud business.Oracle said its backlog stood at $664 billion. About half of that amount is expected to turn into sales over the next 36 months. The company also said much of its newly contracted revenue will not require Oracle to provide all the money needed to build capacity.It expects to rely partly on payments made by customers in advance and on chips supplied by customers themselves.Strong first-quarter earnings and a better balance sheet have also helped Oracle shares recover after a period of weaker performance.Investors have questioned the cost of Oracle’s AI expansion and whether its traditional software business can continue to grow as AI changes the technology industry. “Despite Oracle asking customers to partially fund the technical hardware to alleviate its cash flow pressure, we do not foresee Oracle's cash flow profile changing anytime soon,” Morningstar analyst Luke Yang said as quoted in the Reuters report.“It will take years before (cloud) revenue reaches a scale that supports continuous capacity expansion while generating positive cash flow at the same time.”Oracle also faces risks related to financing and the profitability of its data centers. Component costs have increased, while opposition to data center projects has also grown in the United States. The company has said it plans to raise $40 billion through debt and equity financing during its current fiscal year. That includes a $20 billion stock sale completed during the first quarter.
Article Summary: Oracle said restructuring costs linked to its cost-cutting plan will rise by about $700 million. The higher estimate, which came after the end of Oracle’s August quarter, takes the expected cost of its fiscal 2026 restructuring plan to about $2.8 billion. Oracle said some of the restructuring is linked to the growing use of AI across parts of the company.
